name: Networking Basics
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: A friendly start to networking: devices, layers, IP and subnets, MAC and ARP, DHCP, DNS, ports, TCP, UDP and ping.

lesson.intro: Every app and website rests on a network moving data between devices. This on-ramp covers what networks are made of, the layered model, and how addresses, ARP, DHCP, DNS, ports and routers get a packet to a server and back.
objectives: Tell LANs from WANs and switches from routers
Describe the layers and how data becomes segments, packets and frames
Read an IP address and prefix and say when a host uses its gateway
Explain how ARP, DHCP, DNS, ports, TCP and UDP work together
Use ping and traceroute to find where a connection fails

sections.title: What a network is
sections.key: A network connects devices so they can exchange data: a LAN covers one place, a WAN joins LANs, and the internet is many networks sharing protocols.
sections.body:
You send a photo from your phone to a friend's laptop across the world, and it arrives in a second. Wi-Fi radios, cables, routers and undersea fiber cooperate to get it there.

A **network** is a set of devices connected to exchange data. Laptops, phones, servers and printers are **hosts** (end devices). **Switches** and **routers** in between forward traffic for them.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

The **internet** is a network of networks, run independently and joined by ISPs. Nobody owns it. It works because everyone follows the same **protocols**: agreed rules for addressing, formatting and delivering data.

Most traffic is **client-server**: a client (a browser) asks and a server answers. In **peer to peer** apps each device is both.

[[visual 3]]

items.title: LAN
points: A home, an office floor, a school building
Usually owned by one organization
Ethernet cables and Wi-Fi, fast and cheap

items.title: WAN
points: Connects LANs over long distances
Offices in two cities, for example
Links usually rented from service providers

visual.title: Two LANs joined across the internet
Two measures of performance
rows: How much data a link carries per second
How long one piece of data takes to arrive

sections.pitfall: Mixing up bandwidth and latency. A faster plan (more Mbps) does not cure lag in a game or call; that is latency, which depends mostly on distance and congestion.

check.question: What lets thousands of independently run networks work together as one internet?
choices: One company that owns and manages all the links
Shared protocols that every network follows
A single giant switch in each country
Every device using the same password
check.explanation: No one owns the internet. Networks run by different organizations interoperate because they all speak the same protocols, such as IP for addressing and TCP and UDP for delivery.

sections.title: Network devices and media
sections.key: A switch forwards frames inside a LAN by MAC address; a router forwards packets between networks by IP address and stops broadcasts.
sections.body:
Look behind the desk in a small office and you find the same few boxes. Knowing which does what tells you where to look when something breaks.

[[visual]]

A switch **learns** which device sits on each port from the source MAC address of arriving frames and keeps it in its **MAC address table**. For an unknown destination or a broadcast, it **floods** the frame out every port except the one it came in on. Broadcasts stop at a router: it is the edge of the LAN.

[[visual 2]]

The box from your ISP is several devices in one: a router, a small switch, an access point, a firewall and a DHCP server.

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: The boxes and their jobs
rows: Connects one device to the network; has a hardware **MAC address**
Connects devices within a LAN, forwarding **frames** by MAC address
Connects networks, forwarding **packets** by IP address with its routing table
Lets Wi-Fi devices join a wired LAN
Allows or blocks traffic by security rules
Repeated every signal out every port; replaced by switches

visual.title: Media
rows: Light: far, immune to electrical interference
Radio, shared by every device in range
Laptops and phones; prone to interference

sections.pitfall: Assuming a switch sends every frame to every device. Hubs did that. A switch learns where each MAC lives and forwards only there, flooding only while it does not know yet.

check.question: Which device forwards traffic between your LAN and the internet based on IP addresses?
choices: A switch
A wireless access point
A network interface card
A router
check.explanation: Moving traffic between networks by destination IP address is the router's job. Switches forward within a LAN by MAC address, and access points and NICs only connect devices to the network.

sections.title: Layers and encapsulation
sections.key: Each layer does one job and wraps the data in its own header: ports make a segment, IP addresses a packet, MAC addresses a frame.
sections.body:
Sending a web page means solving many problems at once: which app gets the data, how to recover losses, which path to take, how to put bits on a wire. Networking splits these jobs into **layers**, so Wi-Fi can be swapped for fiber without the browser noticing.

The **TCP/IP model** is what the internet runs. The seven-layer **OSI model** is the vocabulary ("a layer 2 issue").

[[visual]]

On the sender, each layer wraps what it gets from above: **encapsulation**.

[[visual 2]]

The receiver unwraps one header per layer: **decapsulation**. Each device reads only what it needs: a switch the frame (layer 2), a router the packet (layer 3), the receiving host the port (layer 4) to pick the application.

layers.label: Data
layers.detail: the application message, such as an HTTP request

layers.label: Segment
layers.detail: + TCP or UDP header with ports (UDP: datagram)

layers.label: Packet
layers.detail: + IP header with source and destination IP

layers.label: Frame
layers.detail: + Ethernet or Wi-Fi header with MACs, + trailer

sections.deeper: The layers double as a troubleshooting checklist, bottom up. Is the cable plugged in or the Wi-Fi joined (layer 1)? Does the device have a link on the LAN (layer 2)? Does it have a correct IP address and gateway (layer 3)? Is the right port reachable (layer 4)? Does the application answer (layer 7)? Working up the stack keeps you from debugging DNS when the cable is unplugged.
sections.pitfall: Memorizing the seven layer names without their jobs. What matters is which layer reads which address: MAC at layer 2, IP at layer 3, ports at layer 4.

activity.title: Sort it onto a layer
activity.prompt: Place each protocol, device and PDU on its OSI layer. When you are unsure, ask what the item reads or adds: a MAC address points to layer 2, an IP address to layer 3, a port number to layer 4.

check.question: As data goes down the stack, what does the network layer add?
choices: A header with port numbers
A trailer with an error-checking value
A header with source and destination IP addresses
A header with source and destination MAC addresses
check.explanation: The network layer (layer 3) turns a segment into a packet by adding the IP header. Ports belong to the transport header, and MAC addresses and the error-checking trailer belong to the frame at layer 2.

sections.title: IP addresses, subnets and the default gateway
sections.key: An IP address has a network part and a host part, split by the prefix; a host sends to its own subnet directly and everything else to its default gateway.
sections.body:
A MAC address names a device but not where it is. Delivery across the world needs a postal address: the **IP address**.

An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four numbers from 0 to 255: `192.168.1.25`. The **prefix length** splits it into a **network part**, shared by the local network, and a **host part** for one device. /24 is also written as the **subnet mask** `255.255.255.0`.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

To reach beyond its LAN, a host needs an IP address, a mask and a **default gateway** (the local router), plus a DNS server for names.

[[visual 3]]

**Private** ranges are for internal networks and never routed on the internet; the router translates them with NAT. `127.0.0.1` is the **loopback** address: this machine.

[[visual 4]]

IPv4's 4.3 billion addresses ran out years ago. **IPv6** uses 128-bit hex addresses like `2001:db8::10` and runs alongside IPv4.

visual.caption: The first 24 bits are the network (`192.168.1`), the last 8 the host (`.25`).

visual.title: The subnet 192.168.1.0/24
rows: **Network address**: host bits all 0, names the subnet
**Broadcast address**: host bits all 1, every device
visual.caption: h host bits give 2^h addresses, minus those two. A /26 holds 64 addresses; a /23 holds 512, so 10.0.0.0/23 runs from 10.0.0.0 to 10.0.1.255.

visual.title: Where does a host send a packet?

steps.label: Is the destination in my own subnet?
steps.yes: Deliver it directly on the LAN
steps.no: Send it to the default gateway

steps.label: The gateway forwards it toward the other network
steps.detail: The gateway must be inside the host's own subnet, or the host cannot reach it

sections.pitfall: Giving a host the network or broadcast address of its subnet, such as 192.168.1.0 or 192.168.1.255 in a /24. Those two are reserved; usable hosts sit between them.

activity.title: Subnet calculator
activity.prompt: Type 192.168.1.25/24 and check the network, broadcast and host range against the example. Then change only the prefix to /26 and /28 and watch the host count shrink as the network part grows.

check.question: How many usable host addresses does a /24 subnet have?
check.explanation: A /24 leaves 8 host bits, which gives 2^8 = 256 addresses. The network address and the broadcast address are reserved, leaving 254 for hosts.

sections.title: MAC addresses and ARP
sections.key: ARP finds the MAC address that goes with a local IP address; across routers, IP addresses stay the same end to end while MAC addresses change at every hop.
sections.body:
Your laptop knows the printer's IP address, `192.168.1.40`, but Ethernet and Wi-Fi deliver frames by **MAC address**. **ARP** (Address Resolution Protocol) finds the MAC for a local IPv4 address.

A MAC address is 48 bits, written as 12 hex digits: `3c:22:fb:9a:10:4e` (Cisco writes `3c22.fb9a.104e`). The maker assigns it to the NIC; the first half, the **OUI**, names the vendor.

[[visual]]

The answer goes in the **ARP cache**, so later frames go out at once (`ip neigh` on Linux, `arp -a` on Windows).

[[code]]

ARP never crosses a router. For a server on another network, the laptop ARPs for its **default gateway's** MAC and sends the frame there, with the server's IP inside.

[[visual 2]]

messages.note: Who has 192.168.1.40? Tell 192.168.1.20. Every device receives it

messages.label: Store it in the ARP cache

visual.title: Laptop to web server through two routers
visual.caption: Each router strips the frame, picks the next hop and wraps the same packet in a new frame. NAT, which rewrites IP addresses at the network edge, is the common exception.

sections.code:
$ ip neigh
192.168.1.1 dev wlan0 lladdr 3c:22:fb:9a:10:4e REACHABLE
192.168.1.40 dev wlan0 lladdr a4:5e:60:12:7b:01 REACHABLE
sections.pitfall: Expecting a remote server's MAC address in your ARP cache. ARP works only on the local network; for anything beyond it, your host uses the default gateway's MAC.

activity.title: Follow the packet
activity.prompt: Step through the journey hop by hop. At each step, note which addresses change and which stay the same: watch the ARP for the gateway's MAC address, the switch forwarding the frame, and the router putting the same IP packet into a new frame.

check.question: Why is an ARP request sent as a broadcast?
choices: The sender does not know the target's MAC address yet, so it asks everyone
Broadcast frames travel faster than unicast frames on Ethernet
Routers must see every ARP request to update their tables
Only broadcast frames can carry an IP address inside them
check.explanation: Finding the MAC address is the whole point of the request, so the sender cannot address the frame to it. A broadcast reaches every device on the LAN, and only the owner of the IP replies, directly to the sender.

sections.title: DHCP and DNS
sections.key: DHCP gives a new device its IP address, mask, gateway and DNS servers in four messages (DORA); DNS turns names into IP addresses.
sections.body:
Join a cafe's Wi-Fi and within a second your laptop has an IP address, mask, gateway and DNS server, and you typed none of them. **DHCP** hands out these settings. The new device has no address yet, so it starts with broadcasts:

[[visual]]

The address is **leased**: the client renews it while it stays. Servers and printers get fixed or reserved addresses.

If no server answers, the device gives itself a **link-local** address from `169.254.0.0/16` (APIPA on Windows) that works only on the local link. So `169.254.x.x` almost always means DHCP failed.

**DNS** translates names like `example.com` into IP addresses. Your device asks its **resolver**, which walks the hierarchy and caches answers for their TTL:

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

messages.label: Acknowledge
messages.detail: the client starts using the address

messages.note: A PC asks its resolver for shop.example.com
Answers the PC and caches it for the record's TTL

visual.title: DNS records to know
visual.caption: DNS uses port 53, mostly over UDP.

sections.code:
$ dig example.com MX +short
10 mail.example.com.
$ dig example.com AAAA +short
2001:db8::10
sections.pitfall: Treating a 169.254.x.x address as a routing or DNS problem. It means the device never got a DHCP lease, so check the link and the DHCP server first.

check.question: Which settings does a typical DHCP server give a client?
choices: Only an IP address; everything else is typed by hand
A MAC address and a list of open ports
IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS servers
A domain name and a TLS certificate
check.explanation: DHCP delivers the full set a host needs to work beyond its LAN, plus a lease time. MAC addresses come from the NIC itself, not from DHCP.

sections.title: Ports, TCP and UDP
sections.key: A port number picks the application on a host; TCP delivers every byte reliably and in order, while UDP is fast and leaves reliability to the application.
sections.body:
Your laptop has one IP address but runs a browser, chat and music at once. **Port numbers** (16 bits, 0 to 65535) in the transport header tell the operating system which program each piece of data is for.

Servers listen on **well-known ports**, such as HTTPS on 443. The client picks a random high **ephemeral port** as its source, so two tabs to the same server use two source ports and replies reach the right tab. An IP plus a port, like `203.0.113.10:443`, names one end of a conversation.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Neither protocol is better. TCP buys its guarantees with round trips and waiting. In a live call a late packet is useless, so UDP skips the resend.

[[visual 3]]

items.title: TCP
points: Opens with a three-way handshake
Numbers bytes; the receiver acknowledges them
Retransmits lost data, delivers in order
Flow control slows down an overwhelmed receiver
Web, email, SSH, file transfer

items.title: UDP
points: No handshake, no acknowledgments, no retransmission
Small 8-byte header: ports, length, checksum
If a reply is lost, the app just asks again
DNS, DHCP, live voice and video, online games

sections.deeper: Modern protocols blur the line. **QUIC**, the transport under HTTP/3, runs over UDP and builds its own reliability, ordering and encryption in the application, so it can avoid TCP's head-of-line blocking and set up a secure connection in fewer round trips.
sections.pitfall: Calling UDP unreliable as if it were broken. It deliberately leaves reliability to the application, which is right for traffic where late data is useless.

check.question: A laptop opens two browser tabs to the same server on port 443. How are the two TCP connections kept apart?
choices: Each tab gets its own IP address from DHCP
The laptop uses a different source port for each connection
The server gives each tab a different copy of port 443
Both share one connection and are told apart by cookies
check.explanation: A connection is identified by both ends: source IP and port plus destination IP and port. The destination is the same, so the laptop's different ephemeral source ports keep the two connections separate.

sections.title: Routing, NAT, ping and traceroute
sections.key: A router forwards by the longest matching route, NAT lets a whole LAN share one public address, and ping and traceroute show how far packets get.
sections.body:
Once a packet leaves your LAN, each router looks up its destination in the **routing table**: known networks, each reached out a connected interface or via a **next-hop** router. A **default route**, `0.0.0.0/0`, matches everything else.

[[visual]]

A home router's table is little more than its LAN plus a default route to the ISP. A packet that matches nothing is dropped, usually with an ICMP destination unreachable.

Private addresses cannot cross the internet, so the home router does **NAT**: it swaps each private source address for its own public one and tracks conversations by port (**PAT**). Web servers see the router's public IP.

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

[[visual 3]]

visual.title: Which route carries a packet to 10.1.4.7?
rows: Yes, the default route matches anything
visual.caption: When several routes match, the longest prefix wins.

items.title: ping
points: Sends ICMP echo requests, waits for echo replies
Reports the round-trip time
A reply proves the path works both ways
No reply proves little: firewalls often drop ICMP

items.title: traceroute
points: Sends probes with IP TTL 1, then 2, then 3...
Each router lowers the TTL by 1
The router that hits 0 drops it and sends ICMP Time Exceeded, revealing itself
Where replies stop or times jump, look there

steps.label: Check your own settings
steps.detail: `ipconfig` on Windows, `ip addr` and `ip route` on Linux

steps.label: Ping the default gateway
steps.detail: Fails: a local problem (link, address or gateway)

steps.label: Ping a public IP such as 8.8.8.8
steps.detail: Fails: past the gateway (routing or the ISP)

steps.label: Ping a name such as example.com
steps.detail: Fails while the IP works: DNS

steps.label: All pass: test the service itself

sections.pitfall: Concluding a server is down because ping fails. Many hosts and firewalls block ICMP; test the real service, for example with a browser or curl, before deciding.

check.question: What does a router do with a packet that matches no route, when it has no default route either?
choices: Floods it out every interface, like a switch
Sends it back so the sender can try another router
Holds it until a matching route appears
Drops it, usually replying with an ICMP destination unreachable
check.explanation: Routers never flood packets. With no matching route there is nowhere sensible to send it, so the packet is discarded, and the router typically tells the sender with an ICMP unreachable message.

keyTerms.definition: A local area network covering one home, floor or building; WANs connect LANs over distance.
A LAN device that forwards frames by destination MAC address, learning addresses as frames arrive.
A device that forwards packets between networks by destination IP address using a routing table.
Wrapping data in a header at each layer: segment (ports), packet (IP), frame (MAC).
A logical address (32 bits in IPv4) with a network part and a host part.
The split between network and host bits, such as /24 or 255.255.255.0.
The local router a host sends packets to when the destination is outside its own subnet.
A 48-bit hardware address used to deliver frames on the local link.
The protocol that finds the MAC address for an IPv4 address on the local network.
The service that hands out IP address, mask, gateway and DNS settings through Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.
A 16-bit number in the TCP or UDP header that identifies an application on a host.
TCP is connection-oriented and reliable; UDP is connectionless, lightweight and leaves reliability to the app.

summary: A LAN covers one place, WANs join LANs, and the internet is networks sharing protocols.
Switches forward frames by MAC address; routers forward packets by IP address.
Segments carry ports, packets carry IP addresses, frames carry MAC addresses.
Hosts send to their own subnet directly and everything else to the default gateway.
DHCP hands out settings, ARP finds MACs, DNS finds IPs for names.
Ports pick the application; TCP is reliable, UDP is light; ping and traceroute find the break.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend what happens when their laptop on home Wi-Fi sends a request to a website: which addresses it needs, how it gets each one (DHCP, DNS, ARP), and what the home router does to the packet on the way out.

questions.question: Routers forward packets by reading the destination IP address. Which OSI layer number is that?
questions.explanation: IP addressing and routing are layer 3, the Network layer. Layer 2 uses MAC addresses within one local network, and layer 4 adds ports.

questions.question: The TCP/IP model has only 4 layers. Which OSI layers does its Application layer cover?
choices: Only OSI layer 7
OSI layers 4 to 7
OSI layers 5, 6 and 7
OSI layers 6 and 7
questions.explanation: TCP/IP folds OSI's Session (5), Presentation (6) and Application (7) layers into one Application layer. OSI layer 4 (Transport) stays a separate layer in TCP/IP, so 4 to 7 is too many.

questions.question: A laptop sends an HTTP request over Wi-Fi. Going down the stack, what directly wraps the TCP segment?
choices: An Ethernet or Wi-Fi frame, which is then wrapped in an IP packet
An IP packet, which is then wrapped in a Wi-Fi frame
A DNS query, which is then wrapped in an IP packet
Nothing; TCP segments are sent as raw radio signals
questions.explanation: Encapsulation goes transport, then internet, then link: the TCP segment goes inside an IP packet, and the IP packet goes inside a link-layer frame. The frame is the outermost wrapper, not the inner one.

questions.question: How many total IPv4 addresses does a /26 block contain?
questions.explanation: A /26 leaves 32 - 26 = 6 host bits, and 2^6 = 64. Of those, 62 are usable for hosts because the first is the network address and the last is the broadcast address.

questions.question: Which of these is a private IPv4 address that will not be routed on the public internet?
questions.explanation: The private range 172.16.0.0/12 runs from 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255, so 172.20.5.4 is private. 172.32.0.1 sits just past the end of that range, and 193.168.1.1 only looks like the private 192.168.0.0/16 range.

questions.question: Host A has the address 10.0.1.20/23. Which of these addresses is in the same subnet?
questions.explanation: A /23 covers two consecutive /24 blocks. 10.0.1.20/23 is in 10.0.0.0/23, which spans 10.0.0.0 to 10.0.1.255, so 10.0.0.200 is a neighbor. 10.0.2.10 and 10.0.3.1 belong to the next block, 10.0.2.0/23.

questions.question: Why do live video calls usually send media over UDP rather than TCP?
choices: UDP encrypts the media stream by default, unlike TCP
A late packet is useless, so waiting for a resend only adds lag
UDP guarantees packets arrive in order, which video needs
TCP cannot carry audio or video data, only text and files
questions.explanation: In a live call, a frame that arrives late is worse than a frame that never arrives. TCP would pause to resend lost data, causing stutter. UDP does not guarantee order or delivery, and it does not encrypt anything by itself.

questions.question: In the TCP three-way handshake, the client sends SYN first. What does the server send back?
questions.explanation: The server replies SYN-ACK: it acknowledges the client's SYN and sends its own SYN with its starting sequence number. The client then finishes with ACK.

questions.question: Complete the firewall rule so a web server accepts HTTPS connections.
questions.explanation: HTTPS listens on TCP port 443. Port 80 is plain HTTP, 22 is SSH, and 53 is DNS.

questions.question: Which service is paired with its correct default port?
choices: SSH: 23
SMTP: 110
DNS: 53
RDP: 443
questions.explanation: DNS uses port 53. SSH is 22 (23 is Telnet), SMTP is 25 (110 is POP3), and RDP is 3389 (443 is HTTPS).

questions.question: Complete the command to list the mail servers for example.com.
choices: A
CNAME
NS
MX
questions.explanation: MX records name the servers that accept mail for a domain. A returns an IPv4 address, CNAME an alias, and NS the domain's name servers, not its mail servers.

questions.question: A recursive resolver has nothing cached for shop.example.com. Which server does it ask first?
choices: The authoritative server for example.com
A root server
The .com TLD server
Your home router
questions.explanation: With an empty cache, the resolver starts at the top: a root server points it to the .com servers, which point it to example.com's authoritative servers, which return the record. It cannot ask the authoritative server first because it does not yet know where that server is.

questions.question: This DNS record was added so IPv6 visitors can reach the site, but it is rejected. What is wrong?
choices: The TTL of 3600 is too long
The name must not end with a dot
An IPv6 address needs an AAAA record, not an A record
IPv6 addresses must be stored in a CNAME record
questions.explanation: A records hold IPv4 addresses only. IPv6 addresses go in AAAA records. The trailing dot is correct: it marks a fully qualified name, and 3600 seconds is a normal TTL.

questions.question: Your laptop at 192.168.1.20 behind a home router loads a website. What source IP address does the web server see?
choices: 192.168.1.1, the router's inside address
The router's public IP address
questions.explanation: NAT on the router rewrites the private source address to the router's public IP and tracks the connection so the reply returns to your laptop. Private addresses like 192.168.1.20 are never seen on the internet.

questions.question: A router has three routes: 10.0.0.0/8 via A, 10.1.0.0/16 via B, and 0.0.0.0/0 via C. Where does it send a packet for 10.1.4.7?
choices: Via A, because it was the first match
Via B, because it is the most specific match
Via C, because it is the default route
It drops the packet because two routes match
questions.explanation: Routers use longest prefix match. All three routes contain 10.1.4.7, but /16 is longer (more specific) than /8 or /0, so route B wins. The default route is only used when nothing more specific matches.

questions.question: A teammate says the server is down. Based on this output, what is the most likely explanation?
questions.code:
$ ping -c 3 example.com
PING example.com (203.0.113.10): 56 data bytes
Request timeout for icmp_seq 0
Request timeout for icmp_seq 1
Request timeout for icmp_seq 2

$ curl -sI https://example.com | head -1
HTTP/2 200
choices: ICMP is blocked, but the server is up and serving HTTPS
DNS is broken, so example.com cannot be resolved at all
The server is down, and curl only showed a cached copy
Ping fails because it needs TCP port 443 to be open
questions.explanation: The name resolved to 203.0.113.10, so DNS works, and curl got an HTTP 200, so the web server is up. Many firewalls drop ICMP echo requests, which makes ping time out. Ping uses ICMP, which has no ports.

questions.question: How does traceroute discover each router on the path to a destination?
questions.answer: It sends probes with TTL set to 1, then 2, then 3, and so on. Each router that lowers a probe's TTL to 0 drops it and replies with an ICMP Time Exceeded message, which reveals that router's address.
questions.explanation: Traceroute turns the TTL safety mechanism into a measuring tool: probe n expires at hop n, so the replies list the routers in order along with their round-trip times.

questions.question: Which of these is a LAN?
choices: The links joining a company's offices in two cities
The internet as a whole
The wired and Wi-Fi devices on one office floor
A mobile carrier's network across a country
questions.explanation: A LAN covers a small area such as one floor or building. Links between cities form a WAN, and the internet and a national carrier network are collections of many networks.

questions.question: Which of these are end devices (hosts), rather than devices that forward traffic for others? Select all that apply.
choices: A laptop
A network printer
A web server
A switch
A router
questions.explanation: Hosts are where traffic starts and ends: laptops, printers and servers. Switches and routers sit in between and forward traffic for everyone else.

questions.question: Match each device to its job.

pairs.right: Connects devices within a LAN, forwarding frames by MAC address
Connects networks, forwarding packets by IP address
Lets Wi-Fi devices join a wired network
Allows or blocks traffic based on security rules
Connects a single device to the network

questions.explanation: The key pair to keep straight is switch (layer 2, MAC addresses, inside a LAN) versus router (layer 3, IP addresses, between networks).

questions.question: A switch receives a frame whose destination MAC address is not in its MAC address table. What does it do?
choices: Floods it out every port except the one it arrived on
Drops the frame and sends an error to the sender
Sends it to the default gateway to be routed
Holds it until the destination device sends a frame
questions.explanation: An unknown destination is flooded so it still reaches its target. The switch also records the frame's source MAC on the arriving port, and once the destination replies, its address is learned and later frames go out a single port.

questions.question: Put the units in the order they are created as data goes down the stack on the sending host.
items: Segment: a TCP header with ports is added
Packet: an IP header with IP addresses is added
Frame: an Ethernet header and trailer are added
Bits: signals on the wire or the air
questions.explanation: Each layer wraps what the layer above handed it: data into a segment, the segment into a packet, the packet into a frame, and the frame goes out as bits. The receiver unwraps in the reverse order.

questions.question: Which layer adds the port numbers that identify the application?
choices: Network (layer 3)
Data link (layer 2)
Physical (layer 1)
Transport (layer 4)
questions.explanation: Ports live in the TCP or UDP header, which is the transport layer. Layer 3 adds IP addresses and layer 2 adds MAC addresses.

questions.question: A host has the address 192.168.10.37/24. What is the network address of its subnet?
questions.explanation: In a /24 the first three numbers are the network part. Setting the host part to 0 gives the network address, 192.168.10.0, and setting it to 255 gives the broadcast address.

questions.question: A PC is configured as 192.168.1.10/24 with default gateway 192.168.1.1. It sends one packet to 192.168.1.50 and another to 8.8.8.8. Which packets go through the gateway?
choices: Both, because every packet leaves through the gateway
Neither, because the PC can reach both directly
Only the packet to 8.8.8.8
Only the packet to 192.168.1.50
questions.explanation: 192.168.1.50 is inside 192.168.1.0/24, so the PC delivers it directly after an ARP for that host. 8.8.8.8 is outside the subnet, so the PC sends it to the gateway's MAC address and lets the router forward it.

questions.question: This PC can print to a printer on its own subnet but cannot reach anything else. What is wrong?
choices: The mask should be 255.255.0.0 to allow internet access
An address ending in .25 is reserved and cannot be used
Printers block internet access for hosts on their subnet
The default gateway is outside the PC's subnet, so the PC cannot reach it
questions.explanation: With 192.168.1.25/24 the PC can deliver directly only to 192.168.1.x. The gateway 192.168.2.1 is in another subnet, so the PC cannot ARP for it, and every off-subnet packet fails. The gateway is usually 192.168.1.1 here.

questions.question: Before PC A (192.168.1.10) can send its first frame to PC B (192.168.1.20) on the same LAN, what does it need, and how does it get it?
choices: B's MAC address, found with an ARP broadcast
B's port number, found with a DNS query
B's IP address, found with a DHCP request
The gateway's MAC address, found with traceroute
questions.explanation: A already knows B's IP, but a frame needs a destination MAC. A broadcasts an ARP request, B replies with its MAC, and A caches it. The gateway is not involved because B is on the same subnet.

questions.question: A packet travels from your laptop, through two routers, to a web server, with no NAT involved. What happens to its addresses along the way?
choices: The IP addresses change at each router, and the MAC addresses stay the same
The source and destination IPs stay the same, and each hop uses new MAC addresses
Both the IP and the MAC addresses stay the same end to end
Both the IP and the MAC addresses change at every router
questions.explanation: IP addresses identify the two ends of the conversation, so they stay put. MAC addresses only get a frame across one link, so every router builds a new frame with its own MAC as the source and the next hop's MAC as the destination.

questions.question: How many bits long is a MAC address?
questions.explanation: A MAC address is 48 bits, written as 12 hexadecimal digits (each hex digit is 4 bits). An IPv4 address is 32 bits and an IPv6 address 128.

questions.question: Put the four DHCP messages in the order they are exchanged when a laptop joins a network.
items: Discover: the client broadcasts, looking for a DHCP server
Offer: a server proposes an address and settings
Request: the client asks for the offered address
Acknowledge: the server confirms the lease
questions.explanation: DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge. Only after the Acknowledge does the client start using the address.

questions.question: A laptop shows the address 169.254.37.12 and cannot reach anything beyond its local link. What most likely happened?
choices: Its DNS server is returning the wrong addresses
The website it is trying to reach is down
NAT on the router translated its address
No DHCP server answered, so it assigned itself a link-local address
questions.explanation: 169.254.0.0/16 is the link-local range a host picks for itself when DHCP fails. It has no gateway, so nothing beyond the local link works. Check the connection and the DHCP server.

questions.question: Which of these applications typically use UDP? Select all that apply.
choices: DNS lookups
Live voice and video calls
Fast-paced online games
Sending email with SMTP
Logging in with SSH
Downloading a file over HTTP/1.1
questions.explanation: Short queries and real-time media favor UDP: a lost DNS reply is simply asked again, and a late video frame is useless anyway. Email, SSH and HTTP/1.1 downloads need every byte in order, so they use TCP.

questions.question: On Linux or macOS, type the command that lists the routers on the path to example.com.
questions.explanation: traceroute sends probes with increasing TTL values and prints each router that answers with Time Exceeded. On Windows the same tool is tracert example.com.

questions.question: Based on this output, what is the most likely problem?
questions.code:
$ ping -c 1 8.8.8.8
64 bytes from 8.8.8.8: icmp_seq=1 ttl=117 time=12.3 ms

$ ping -c 1 example.com
ping: example.com: Name or service not known
choices: Name resolution: DNS is not working
The default gateway is unreachable
The network cable is unplugged
The ISP is blocking all ICMP traffic
questions.explanation: Replies from 8.8.8.8 prove the link, the gateway and internet routing all work, and ICMP is clearly allowed. Only the name lookup failed, so check the DNS server settings.
